name: Felix Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead breakfast at a busy restaurant by the station. I start the ovens, check deliveries, cook eggs to order and teach the newer cooks to keep raw and ready-to-eat food apart. I have a vocational cooking certificate, and I take pride in sending the first table out before their train leaves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How is the job working for you outside the kitchen?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and share a rented flat with my partner, who works part time at a bookshop. I am one of the stronger cooks here, yet the lead wage is low, we have three weeks of expenses saved, and there are few other kitchens along our bus route. I use AI every day to draft prep counts from past sales and sometimes sketch menus, but I weigh the food, check allergens and never put customer details into the tool.

I'd use **AI prep lists** only as drafts.
think: Our **three-week reserve** and variable bookshop wage leave little room for late pay.
I expect **paid breakfasts** to continue under modest AI.
do: Confirm **next month's breakfasts** and dated wage sheet.
Check **AI prep counts** against stock and labels; use sales totals without names and sign actual temperatures.
feel: I feel **anxious** about household cash despite steady customers.
S0.quote: A computer can count eggs without paying our rent.
fieldNote: His **lead breakfast skill** earns low pay in a town with few other kitchen posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that AI can lay out a prep list, but the cook at the serving counter still decides what is safe to serve. I would keep the breakfast rota and the allergen book where everyone can see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's bookshop hours vary and our three-week reserve is small. If change stays mild, I expect breakfast customers and my paid line hours to continue, but a late wage is still hard to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm the next month's paid breakfasts and get the manager to date the wage sheet. In the first year of mild AI I'll continue my daily prep-count tool only with our own sales totals, cross-check stock and allergy labels by hand, and have the opening cook sign the real temperature readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our short reserve, even if breakfast stays busy. A computer can count eggs without paying our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was a prep count wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday it forecast forty croissants, but a rail strike left twenty on the rack. We adjusted the next tray by looking at the queue, not at the old chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do customer names go into the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I use totals from our till, not customer names or orders. If the manager asks for personal data, I will leave that field blank.

say: I'd trial **new ordering software** with a named cook checking food.
I'd ask whether **paid opening hours** will change.
think: The system could remove **one paid hour** while breakfast work stays.
A **lead raise** remains unpromised, even with better counts.
do: Compare **four weeks' opening pay** and waste with the manager.
Learn **new AI forecasting** only in paid licensed trial with nameless data and manual stock/allergen checks.
Request **written cooking rota** and stop unpaid testing if paid opening hour disappears.
feel: I feel **anxious** about one realistic lost hour despite liking useful tools.
S1.quote: I cannot afford to donate an hour testing an AI ordering tool.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** makes a new forecast trial plausible, but not an unpaid shift.
He **checks swapped pastries** and allergen labels despite any accurate-looking order screen.

steps.text: Compare four weeks of paid opening hours and food waste with manager
Learn new AI forecasting in paid licensed trial with nameless data and manual stock/allergen checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether software will set the ordering and rota as well as the prep list. I would offer to test it, provided a named cook still checks deliveries and allergens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new ordering system could remove my paid opening hour even while I cook the same breakfasts. I could use better counts to argue for a proper lead wage, but the manager has promised neither hours nor a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll compare four weeks of opening-hour pay and food waste with the manager. In the first year I'll learn the new AI forecasting screen that drafts stock orders only during a paid trial with an approved licence, no customer names and a manual stock and allergen check; if it removes my paid hour without replacement, I'll ask for a written cooking rota and stop unpaid testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real hour of pay disappearing. I like a useful tool, but I cannot afford to donate an hour testing an AI ordering tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can a forecast miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supplier sometimes swaps a nut-containing pastry without saying so on the order screen. I would read the packaging and ask the chef before putting it on the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would lower waste mean a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a lower waste figure alone does not guarantee a raise. I would ask the manager for a written wage and hours before counting any gain.

S2.quote: Three weeks saved cannot make me brave about a missing wage line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the breakfast crew thinking AGI by 2028 may set orders and shifts, while capable cooking robots follow around 2031. I would ask for paid manual checks before anyone lets a robot near a hot tray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the opening-hour premium to go when ordering becomes automatic in 2028. A machine that can cook is three years later, so my line job is not gone that morning, but the reserve will still be only three weeks if we cannot save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll get the opening premium and next season's shifts in writing and ask the manager whether a paid equipment-safety trial exists. In the first year after 2028 I'll keep cooking booked breakfasts and accept any AI ordering only with a paid human check of delivered food and allergies; if the premium ends, I'll ask the manager for a written replacement hour, and I will not touch an unguarded hot machine for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the premium I expect to lose and the later robot risk. Three weeks saved cannot make me brave about a missing wage line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a paid safety trial been offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, no safety trial has been funded yet. I can ask what it would pay, but I will not call it a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check a robot's guards, emergency stop and hot surface with the trained lead before service, if such a machine arrives. A tablet order cannot tell me whether a child has a sesame allergy.

say: I'd ask for **paid guarded training** ahead of 2034 cooking robots.
I'd keep **breakfast safety** with trained humans.
think: The **planning hour** may go before 2031 and robots could later take simple cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner that full AGI by 2031 leaves a few years to prepare for cooking robots around 2034. I would rather train on a guarded machine in paid time than learn by burning somebody at breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the planning hour will vanish before 2031 and a robot might later take the simple egg station. A new equipment-monitor role could pay, but I need a real post and training I can afford without losing current wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the restaurant group and training centre whether any actual paid kitchen-equipment monitor vacancy is posted and accepts my cooking certificate plus their safety course. I'll take the course only after such a posting accepts both qualifications and a funded place pays my training hours, my breakfast wage is protected and the course includes supervised guards, emergency stops, cleaning and allergen checks; in the first year after 2031 I'll keep paid cooking and apply to that actual posted paid role only after completing the accepted training and qualifying, written net pay after the bus replaces my full present weekly take-home and both start and home buses work, staying until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a likely opening-hour loss and later egg-station risk. I am curious about the equipment. Curiosity does not cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a monitor vacancy posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No one has posted the monitor vacancy today. If the course is not accepted or the training hours are unpaid, I will keep breakfast shifts and skip it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who supervises the hot equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer would have to show me how to isolate power before cleaning and have a qualified lead watch me practise. I would not sign off a guard or an allergen meal alone.

I'd ask for a **written lead rate** now.
think: At **37**, I would still want paid kitchen work.
Our **three-week cushion** today cannot carry an unpaid wage promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that full AGI by 2036 gives me a decade to build a safer work record, with cooking robots around 2039. I still want every kitchen to name the human who can stop a hot machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I would rather supervise safe breakfasts than retire from cooking. If the restaurant can still pay a proper rate, I may stay, but three weeks saved today is too little to wait for a promised wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask for a written lead rate and put any genuinely extra paid holiday shifts after rent, food and bus fares into a one-month emergency fund. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid breakfast work only with trained human checks of guards, hot surfaces and allergens; if the paid line shrinks, I'll seek a posted qualified kitchen-safety or cooking role only with written net after travel replacing my full present weekly take-home, buses for the start and home journey and a signed offer before I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about current low pay and the short reserve, even with ten years to make choices. I would feel steadier once the emergency fund really reaches a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra shift pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra holiday shift pays, no money moves into that fund. The rent and groceries are paid before any target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can your partner cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the bookshop cannot promise more hours either. We would use the written wage and bus timetable, not a story about robots, to decide whether I can change kitchens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the opening premium could go before there is a funded robot-safety job. Written paid shifts and a supervised course tied to a real post would help, as would a month of expenses actually saved.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask which cook gets the authority to press stop when the egg robot misreads a tray. A kitchen cannot run safely on a diagram of breakfast.

headlineQuote: A kitchen cannot run safely on a diagram of breakfast.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old breakfast lead** with a vocational cooking certificate and a partner.
His **low pay**, three-week reserve and few nearby kitchens make one lost opening hour consequential.
He **uses AI daily** for nameless prep counts but checks food and temperatures himself.
He explores **funded equipment training** only with protected wages, supervision and a qualifying paid post.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Felix's opening premium before 2031 cooking robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid shifts**, a supervised course linked to a real post and an actual one-month reserve would help.
